items.prose: A small lender has eight past loans, each with the number of missed payments in the year before and whether the borrower defaulted. The rule is **default when missed payments are at least $t$**.

parts.question: How many of the eight loans does $t$ = 3 get right?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the rule to each loan and count agreements.

byKey.wrong-count: 3 is how many it gets wrong: loans 2, 4 and 7.
byKey.strict: You treated 3 missed payments as below the threshold. At least 3 includes 3, so loan 4 is called a default and is wrong.

explain.text: Below 3 the rule says no default: right for loans 1 and 3, wrong for loan 2. From 3 up it says default: right for loans 5, 6 and 8, wrong for 4 and 7. That is $2 + 3 = 5$.

parts.question: Part 1 found 5 right at $t$ = 3. Which whole-number $t$ from 0 to 10 gets the most loans right?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score the thresholds near the middle and keep the best.

byKey.three: $t$ = 3 gets 5. Moving to 4 fixes loan 4, which had 3 missed payments and did not default.
byKey.half: $t$ = 5 gets 5: it misses loan 5, which defaulted after 4 missed payments.

explain.text: $t$ = 3 gets 5, $t$ = 4 gets 6 and $t$ = 5 gets 5; the others do worse. Only loans 2 and 7 are wrong at $t$ = 4.

parts.question: Using $t$ = 4 from part 2, what is its accuracy on the eight training loans, as a percentage?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the number right by 8.

byKey.count: You typed the count, 6, as a percentage. Divide by 8 first.

explain.text: 6 of the 8 loans are right, so the training accuracy is $\tfrac{6}{8} = 75\%$.

parts.question: Four more loans were kept back: missed payments 2, 5, 8 and 10. The first three defaulted and the last did not. Using $t$ = 4, what is the test score, as a percentage?

feedback.correct: Right on 5 and 8, wrong on 2 and 10: 50%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply $t$ = 4 to each kept-back loan, then divide by 4.

byKey.train: 75% is the training score from part 3. The test score uses the four kept-back loans.
byKey.one: 25% is 1 right. Check the loans with 5 and 8 missed payments: both defaulted and both are called defaults.

explain.text: $t$ = 4 calls 5, 8 and 10 defaults and 2 not. It is wrong on 2 (a default missed) and 10 (did not default). That is $\tfrac{2}{4} = 50\%$, below the 75% from training.

parts.question: A memoriser stored the eight training loans by missed payments. How many of the four kept-back loans from part 4 can it answer at all?

feedback.correct: Only the loan with 2 missed payments: 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which of 2, 5, 8 and 10 appear among the training loans?

byKey.all: It only answers counts it stored. 5, 8 and 10 never appeared.
byKey.rule-right: 2 is how many the rule gets right. The memoriser answers only 1.

explain.text: The training loans have 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9 missed payments. Of 2, 5, 8 and 10, only 2 is there. So the memoriser answers 1 of 4.

items.prose: A café wants to know each evening whether tomorrow will be busy, so it can call in extra staff. The manager's old rule was **busy on Saturdays**. Now it has a year of days like these.

parts.question: Is the manager's rule, busy on Saturdays, a program or a model?

options.text: A program: a person wrote it
A model: it was found from past days
options.why: The manager wrote it from a hunch. No examples chose it.

feedback.correct: A person wrote it, so it is a program.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask who chose the rule.

explain.text: The manager typed the rule from experience. A model would have its rule chosen by the year of past days.

parts.question: Using the table, which column is the label for tomorrow's model?

options.why: Covers served is a number about the same day. It is not the yes or no answer the café wants.
Bookings are known the evening before: a feature.
The day type is known in advance: a feature.

feedback.correct: Busy? is the answer the café wants.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which column is the yes or no answer?

explain.text: The café wants a yes or no for tomorrow. Busy? is that answer, so it is the label.

parts.question: With Busy? as the label from part 2, which column is a leak?

options.why: Bookings by 6 pm the day before are known by the evening: fair.
The forecast is out the evening before: fair.
The day type is always known in advance.

feedback.correct: Covers served is only known after the day.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which number does not exist the evening before?

explain.text: Covers served is counted at closing time tomorrow. It nearly gives the label away and is not known in the evening, so it is a leak.

parts.question: Leave out the label from part 2 and the leak from part 3. How many features does each day have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take two columns away from five.

byKey.with-leak: You kept Covers served. It is the leak, so it goes.
byKey.all: Five is every column, label included.

explain.text: Five columns less the label and the leak leaves $5 - 2 = 3$ features: day type, forecast and bookings.

parts.question: A model using those 3 features, chosen on 300 days, gets 17 of 20 kept-back days right. What is its test score, as a percentage?

byKey.count: You typed 17 as a percentage. Divide by 20 first.

explain.text: The 20 kept-back days were never used to choose, so $\tfrac{17}{20} = 85\%$ is an honest test score.

items.prose: A desk tests the rule **buy when the signal is above the cut-off** on ten past days, with three cut-offs: 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Five later days are kept back.

parts.question: How many of the ten training days does the cut-off 0.2 get right?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count right buys and right non-buys.

byKey.wrong-count: 4 is how many it gets wrong: days 2, 4, 8 and 10.
byKey.buys: 9 is the number of buys. Four of those days did not rise.

explain.text: Above 0.2 are nine days: five rose and four did not. Below is day 1 only, which did not rise, so it is right. That is $5 + 1 = 6$ of 10.

parts.question: Part 1 found 6 right at 0.2. Which of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 is best on the training days? Give the cut-off as a decimal.

feedback.correct: 0.5 gets 7 of 10; the other two get 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Score all three cut-offs on the ten days.

byKey.low: 0.2 gets 6. It buys on days 2, 4, 8 and 10, which did not rise; 0.5 skips days 2 and 8.
byKey.high: 0.8 gets 6: it skips days 3, 5 and 9, which all rose.

explain.text: 0.2 and 0.8 each get 6 of 10, and 0.5 gets 7. It buys on days 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10, and four of those rose. It is right on three of the four days it skips.

parts.question: Using 0.5 from part 2, score it once on the five kept-back days below. What is its test score, as a percentage?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply 0.5 to each kept-back day, then divide by 5.

byKey.train: 70% is its training score. The test score uses the five kept-back days.

explain.text: 0.5 buys on days 13 and 14: day 14 rose, day 13 did not. It skips days 11, 12 and 15: day 11 did not rise, but 12 and 15 did. That is 2 of 5, or 40%.

parts.question: A colleague scores all three cut-offs on the five kept-back days and reports the best. What score do they report, as a percentage?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 on the five days and keep the best.

byKey.honest: 40% is the honest score of 0.5 from part 3. The colleague picks the best of three, which is higher.
byKey.mid: 60% is 0.8's score, 3 of 5. 0.2 does better, with 4.

explain.text: On the five days, 0.2 gets 4, 0.5 gets 2 and 0.8 gets 3. The colleague reports the best, $\tfrac{4}{5} = 80\%$.

parts.question: Which figure is an honest estimate of how the desk's chosen rule will do on new days?

options.why: The five days chose that cut-off, so 80% is a training score in disguise.
The ten training days chose 0.5, so 70% flatters it.

feedback.correct: 40%: 0.5 was chosen without the kept-back days and scored on them once.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which figure comes from days that played no part in choosing?

explain.text: Only part 3 scores a rule on days that did not choose it. The 70% and the 80% both come from days that picked the cut-off. Five days is still a small test, so 40% is rough.
